blocks.text: Pleural effusion is the abnormal accumulation of fluid within the pleural cavity, between the visceral and parietal pleura.
Normally, a small quantity of fluid is present in the pleural space to facilitate friction-free movement of the lungs during respiration.

blocks.title: Excess accumulation occurs when there is:

items.text: Movement of fluid from the peritoneal cavity.
Inflammation or infection of the pleural space.

blocks.text: Empyema thoracis is the accumulation of frank pus within the pleural cavity, usually resulting from bacterial infection.

blocks.title: It commonly develops as a complication of:

items.text: Parapneumonic effusion describes pleural fluid associated with pneumonia.
Complicated parapneumonic effusion describes infected pleural fluid requiring drainage or other source control.
Empyema describes frank pus in the pleural cavity.

blocks.text: B. Based on aetiology

items.text: Infective: bacterial pneumonia, tuberculosis, fungal infections.

content_groups.group_title: 1.4 Classification of parapneumonic effusion and empyema

blocks.text: The disease progresses through three stages.
Stage 1: Exudative stage
Sterile inflammatory fluid.

items.text: Usually responds to antibiotics without drainage if uncomplicated.

blocks.text: Stage 2: Fibrinopurulent stage

items.text: Reduced pleural fluid pH and glucose.
Usually requires antibiotics and pleural drainage.

blocks.text: Stage 3: Organising stage

items.text: Formation of a thick pleural peel.

blocks.text: Light's criteria distinguish transudative from exudative pleural effusions.
An effusion is classified as exudative if at least ONE of the following criteria is met:

items.text: Pleural fluid protein / serum protein ratio greater than 0.5.
Pleural fluid LDH / serum LDH ratio greater than 0.6.
Pleural fluid LDH greater than two-thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH.

blocks.text: If none is met, the effusion is classified as transudative.
Clinical application

Important exception: Diuretic-treated heart failure can produce a pseudo-exudate. If the clinical picture suggests heart failure despite exudative Light's criteria, consider the serum–pleural albumin gradient. A gradient greater than 1.2 g/dL supports a transudative mechanism.
Diagnostic thoracentesis is indicated for most unexplained unilateral effusions and suspected pleural infections, provided there is a safely accessible fluid pocket.

blocks.title: Pleural TB is usually paucibacillary. Therefore:

items.text: Pleural fluid cytology is the initial investigation.

content_groups.group_title: 4.3 Treatment of complicated parapneumonic effusion and empyema

blocks.text: Indications for chest tube drainage

items.text: Frank pus in the pleural space.
Positive pleural fluid Gram stain or culture in an appropriate clinical context.
Clinical evidence of pleural infection with an inadequately drained collection.

blocks.text: For intermediate pH of greater than 7.20 but less than 7.40, consider drainage if LDH is above 900 IU/L, particularly with low glucose, persistent fever, large fluid volume or ultrasound septations.
For pH of 7.40 or higher, immediate drainage is generally unnecessary unless other compelling findings indicate infection requiring source control.

items.text: Small-bore chest tube (14 French or smaller) is recommended as the initial drainage approach for most adult pleural infections.
Ultrasound guidance should be used where appropriate.
Connect to a closed drainage system.
Monitor the quantity and character of drainage.
Confirm tube position and lung response through imaging.

blocks.text: Do not routinely use large-bore drains simply because the fluid is infected. Larger tubes may be required in selected situations, such as substantial haemothorax or when small-bore drainage is inadequate.
For patients with residual loculated pleural infection despite appropriate chest tube drainage, consider combined tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) and DNase.
Recommended combination
Adult regimen:
The two drugs are administered separately through the chest tube according to the institutional pleural protocol, with an appropriate dwell period and subsequent drainage.

items.text: Assess bleeding risk and anticoagulation before administration.

blocks.text: A reduced tPA dose of 5 mg twice daily may be considered in selected patients with increased bleeding risk, under specialist supervision.

items.text: Persistent infected collection despite adequate drainage.

A. Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS)
B. Decortication
Surgical removal of the fibrous pleural peel to permit lung re-expansion.

VATS is generally preferred over open thoracotomy when surgical management is appropriate.
